claim: Varroa destructor mites can cause honeybee colonies to collapse by spreading viruses and feeding on the fat reserves of adults and larvae.
source: They can cause colonies to collapse by spreading viruses and feeding on the fat reserves of adults and larvae.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about the biological impact of Varroa mites on honeybee colonies.

claim: Amitraz is used to control Varroa mites due to its low toxicity to bees.
source: Amitraz is used to control mites due to its low toxicity to bees
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established practice in pest management.

claim: Amitraz and its major metabolite potently activated all four mite octopamine receptors.
source: In this study, we found that amitraz and its major metabolite potently activated all four mite octopamine receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study, specifically the dose-response curves shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Octβ2R is the sole target of amitraz in vivo.
source: Behavioral assays using Drosophila null mutants of octopamine receptors identified one receptor subtype Octβ2R as the sole target of amitraz in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays showing that only octβ2R mutants were insensitive to amitraz (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Thermogenetic activation of octβ2R-expressing neurons mimics amitraz poisoning symptoms in target pests.
source: We found that thermogenetic activation of octβ2R-expressing neurons mimics amitraz poisoning symptoms in target pests.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using TRPA1-mediated activation shown in Figure 4 and associated videos.

claim: The mite Octβ2R was more sensitive to amitraz and its metabolite than the bee Octβ2R.
source: We next confirmed that the mite Octβ2R was more sensitive to amitraz and its metabolite than the bee Octβ2R in pharmacological assays and transgenic flies.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5A and 5B, and behavioral data in Figure 6.

claim: Replacement of three bee-specific residues with the counterparts in the mite receptor increased amitraz sensitivity of the bee Octβ2R.
source: Furthermore, replacement of three bee-specific residues with the counterparts in the mite receptor increased amitraz sensitivity of the bee Octβ2R
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data (Figure 5A) and behavioral assays in transgenic flies (Figure 6).

claim: The relative insensitivity of the bee Octβ2R receptor is the major mechanism for honeybees to resist amitraz.
source: indicating that the relative insensitivity of their receptor is the major mechanism for honeybees to resist amitraz.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined pharmacological and genetic evidence showing differential receptor sensitivity.

claim: Large colony losses of honeybees have been reported worldwide over the last few decades in large part due to colony collapse disorder.
source: However, large colony losses have been reported worldwide over the last few decades in large part due to a syndrome called colony collapse disorder (Ratnieks and Carreck, 2010; Tylianakis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Factors that contribute to colony collapse disorder include land-use intensification, pesticides, and the parasitic mite Varroa destructor.
source: Factors that appear to contribute to colony collapse disorder and global bee decline include land‐use intensification, pesticides (Martin et al., 2012; Woodcock et al., 2017), and the parasitic mite Varroa destructor, which transmits pathogens (Stokstad, 2019; Wilfert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Varroa mites are the most destructive pest of managed honeybee colonies.
source: Varroa mites colonize beehives and are the most destructive pest of managed honeybee colonies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Commercial beekeepers rely on chemical control agents against Varroa mites including tau-fluvalinate, coumaphos, and amitraz.
source: Currently, only a few synthetic insecticides/acaricides are employed for this purpose such as tau-fluvalinate, coumaphos, and amitraz (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Excessive dependence on tau-fluvalinate and coumaphos has led to high levels of resistance and loss of effectiveness.
source: Excessive dependence on tau-fluvalinate and coumaphos has led to high levels of resistance and loss of effectiveness (González-Cabrera et al., 2016; Higes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Wide-ranging amitraz resistance is rare.
source: In contrast, wide-ranging amitraz resistance is rare.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the field.

claim: Amitraz is still effective in controlling Varroa populations in commercial beekeeping operations.
source: Consequently, amitraz is still effective in controlling Varroa populations in commercial beekeeping operations (Kamler et al., 2016; Rinkevich, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The P450 inhibitor piperonyl butoxide elevated the toxicity of tau-fluvalinate and coumaphos in bees.
source: Previous studies found that the P450 inhibitor piperonyl butoxide elevated the toxicity of tau-fluvalinate and coumaphos in bees (Johnson et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2009) by inhibiting three P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP9Q family (Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: No metabolite enzyme inhibitors enhance the toxicity of amitraz to honeybees.
source: On the other hand, no metabolite enzyme inhibitors enhance the toxicity of amitraz to honeybees (Johnson et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Pharmacological differences of the molecular target rather than metabolic detoxication may account for the bee's resistance to amitraz.
source: indicating that pharmacological differences of the molecular target rather than metabolic detoxication may account for the bee's resistance to amitraz.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that enzyme inhibitors do not enhance amitraz toxicity in bees.

claim: Amitraz is particularly effective against mites and ticks, as well as first instar larvae of lepidoptera.
source: Amitraz is particularly effective against mites and ticks, as well as first instar larvae of lepidoptera (Hollingworth, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Amitraz can mimic the actions of octopamine, the invertebrate analog of norepinephrine.
source: Like other formamidines, amitraz can mimic the actions of octopamine (OA), the invertebrate analog of norepinephrine (Evans and Gee, 1980; Hollingworth and Murdock, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Amitraz acts as a high-affinity agonist of OA receptors, which belong to the family of rhodopsin-like G protein coupled receptors.
source: It acts as a high-affinity agonist of OA receptors, which belong to the family of rhodopsin-like G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about amitraz's mechanism of action.

claim: There are at least four classes of OA receptors in invertebrates: Octα1R, Octα2R, OctβR, and Oct-TyrR.
source: In invertebrates, there are at least four classes of OA receptors: Octα1R (α1-adrenergic-like octopamine receptor, also referred to as OAMB or OA1), Octα2R (α2-adrenergic-like octopamine receptor, also referred to as OA3), OctβR (β-adrenergic-like octopamine receptor, also referred to as OA2), and Oct-TyrR (octopamine/tyramine receptor, also referred to as TAR1) (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Point mutations in the Octβ2R or Oct-TyrR were found in amitraz-resistant strains of the cattle tick Rhipicephalus microplus.
source: Amitraz is also used to control the cattle tick, Rhipicephalus microplus, and point mutations in the Octβ2R or Oct-TyrR were found in resistant strains (Baron et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2007; Corley et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Four Varroa OA receptors were identified: VdOAMB, VdOctα2R, VdOct-TyrR, and VdOctβ2R.
source: We identified four candidate Varroa OA receptors, which have amino acid homology to the Drosophila counterparts VdOAMB (33% identical; 81% coverage), VdOctα2R (61% identical; 44% coverage), VdOct-TyrR (56% identical; 52% coverage), and VdOctβ2R (56% identical; 63% coverage) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All four Varroa OA receptors were functional and showed dose-dependent responses to OA when expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: When expressed in HEK293 cells, all receptors were functional and showed dose-dependent responses to OA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: VdOctβ2R has an EC50 of 72.8 nM for amitraz.
source: Dose-response analysis showed that VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 72.8 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 90.2 nM) were more sensitive to amitraz compared to VdOAMB (EC50 = 499.5 nM) and VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 548.2 nM) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VdOctα2R has an EC50 of 90.2 nM for amitraz.
source: Dose-response analysis showed that VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 72.8 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 90.2 nM) were more sensitive to amitraz compared to VdOAMB (EC50 = 499.5 nM) and VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 548.2 nM) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VdOAMB has an EC50 of 499.5 nM for amitraz.
source: Dose-response analysis showed that VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 72.8 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 90.2 nM) were more sensitive to amitraz compared to VdOAMB (EC50 = 499.5 nM) and VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 548.2 nM) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VdOct-TyrR has an EC50 of 548.2 nM for amitraz.
source: Dose-response analysis showed that VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 72.8 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 90.2 nM) were more sensitive to amitraz compared to VdOAMB (EC50 = 499.5 nM) and VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 548.2 nM) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VdOctβ2R has an EC50 of 6.9 nM for DPMF.
source: However, VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 6.9 nM) and VdOAMB (EC50 = 5.2 nM) were more sensitive to DPMF compared to VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 49.3 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 190.2 nM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: VdOAMB has an EC50 of 5.2 nM for DPMF.
source: However, VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 6.9 nM) and VdOAMB (EC50 = 5.2 nM) were more sensitive to DPMF compared to VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 49.3 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 190.2 nM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: VdOct-TyrR has an EC50 of 49.3 nM for DPMF.
source: However, VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 6.9 nM) and VdOAMB (EC50 = 5.2 nM) were more sensitive to DPMF compared to VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 49.3 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 190.2 nM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: VdOctα2R has an EC50 of 190.2 nM for DPMF.
source: However, VdOctβ2R (EC50 = 6.9 nM) and VdOAMB (EC50 = 5.2 nM) were more sensitive to DPMF compared to VdOct-TyrR (EC50 = 49.3 nM) and VdOctα2R (EC50 = 190.2 nM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Three out of four Varroa receptors showed higher potency and efficacy to DPMF than amitraz.
source: In addition, although three out of four of these Varroa receptors showed higher potency and efficacy to DPMF than amitraz, both chemicals were very effective.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the EC50 values for amitraz and DPMF across the four receptors shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: An I61F amino acid substitution in the Octβ2R of the cattle tick R. microplus is associated with amitraz resistance.
source: An I61F amino acid substitution in the Octβ2R of the cattle tick, R. microplus, is associated with amitraz resistance (Corley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The wild-type and I61F mutant of RmOctβ2R were not functional when expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: We expressed the wild-type and I61F mutant of RmOctβ2R in HEK293 cells, but they were not functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The isoleucine residue in transmembrane domain 1 (TM1) is conserved in all representative invertebrate species.
source: We found that this residue in transmembrane domain 1 (TM1) is conserved in all representative invertebrate species (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no significant difference in the EC50 between the wild-type VdOctβ2R and the I40F mutant for amitraz and DPMF.
source: However, there was no significant difference in the EC50 between the wild-type and mutant receptors (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Amitraz has low toxicity to wild-type flies as even 5 mM amitraz caused no significant lethality after 4 days of exposure.
source: We found that amitraz has low toxicity to wild-type flies as even 5 mM amitraz caused no significant lethality after they were exposed to an amitraz diet for 4 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with chlorodimeform reduces fighting latency and increases the lunging frequency in socially grouped flies.
source: It is reported that treatment with chlorodimeform, another formamidine insecticide and octopaminergic agonist, reduces fighting latency and increases the lunging frequency in socially grouped flies (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Treatment of group-housed wild-type Canton-S flies with 1 mM amitraz resulted in more aggressive behaviors, with males markedly increasing their lunging frequency and decreasing their fighting latency.
source: In comparison to control flies, treatment of group-housed wide-type Canton-S flies with amitraz resulted in more aggressive behaviors. Males markedly increased their lunging frequency and decreased their fighting latency (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: All OA receptor mutants except octβ2Rf05679 showed robust male-male aggression when treated with amitraz.
source: We then applied amitraz to six OA receptor mutants and found that all but the octβ2R null allele octβ2Rf05679 showed robust male-male aggression, as seen in the wide-type animals (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Males with octβ2Rf05679 combined with a corresponding deficiency were not affected by amitraz.
source: We also combined octβ2Rf05679 with a corresponding deficiency (Df) that uncovers this gene and found that these males were also not affected by amitraz (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Heterozygous control males were still responsive to amitraz.
source: However, heterozygous control males were still responsive to amitraz (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Wild-type flies exhibited hyperactivity when fed with 100 μM or 1 mM amitraz.
source: When we added 100 μM or 1 mM amitraz to the diet of agarose-sucrose medium (2% agarose and 5% sucrose), wide-type flies exhibited hyperactivity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: octβ2Rf05679 flies showed no elevation in locomotor activity upon amitraz treatment, while other receptor mutants exhibited an increase in locomotion.
source: Same as above, octβ2Rf05679 flies showed no elevation in locomotor activity, while other receptor mutants exhibited an increase in locomotion upon amitraz treatment (Figure 3B-G).
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figures 3B-G.

claim: Octβ2R is the only receptor that mediates the effects of amitraz in vivo.
source: Therefore, Octβ2R is the only receptor that mediates the effects of amitraz in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral resistance of octβ2R mutants to amitraz while other receptor mutants remained sensitive.

claim: At sublethal doses, formamidines cause abnormal behaviors like dispersal from plants and detachment of ticks from their host, presumably induced by higher motor activity.
source: At sublethal doses, these insecticides cause abnormal behaviors like dispersal from plants and detachment of ticks from their host, presumably induced by higher motor activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about formamidine insecticides.

claim: At higher doses, formamidine-induced hyperactivity can induce tremors that lead to death.
source: At higher doses, this hyperactivity can induce tremors that lead to death (Evans and Gee, 1980; Stone et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Octβ2R is coupled to Gs, which typically leads to neuronal activation.
source: Octβ2R is coupled to Gs, which typically leads to neuronal activation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about GPCR signaling.

claim: Expressing trpA1 in octβ2R-Gal4 neurons strongly induced hyperactivity behavior at 32℃ and eventually led to paralysis.
source: We found that expressing trpA1 in octβ2R-Gal4 neurons strongly induced hyperactivity behavior at 32℃ and eventually led to paralysis ( Figure 4—video 1 and Figure 4—video 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and associated videos.

claim: Activation of oamb-Gal4 and oct-tyrRGal4 neurons did not show any behavioral defects.
source: We also expressed trpA1 in oamb-Gal4, oct-tyrRGal4, and octα2R-Gal4 neurons and found that activation of oamb-Gal4 and oct-tyrRGal4 neurons did not show any behavioral defects (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Activation of octα2R-Gal4 neurons induced knock-down effects, with flies being directly paralyzed without hyperactivity.
source: Although activation of octα2R-Gal4 neurons also induced knock-down effects, flies were directly paralyzed without hyperactivity ( , Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and associated video.

claim: Octα2R is a Gi-coupled receptor that decreases cAMP upon activation, which is associated with neuronal silencing.
source: Since Octα2R is a Gi-coupled receptor, to decrease cAMP upon activation (Qi et al., 2017), which is associated with neuronal silencing
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Silencing of octα2R-Gal4 neurons produced a 'stop' behavior rather than hyperactivity or paralysis.
source: However, silencing of octα2R-Gal4 neurons produced a 'stop' behavior rather than hyperactivity or paralysis. The flies exhibited almost no translational or rotational body movement (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 1.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of octβ2R-expressing neurons phenocopies the action of amitraz in target pests.
source: Therefore, thermogenetic activation of octβ2R-expressing neurons in a short time window phenocopies the action of amitraz in target pests
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between the behavioral effects of TRPA1-mediated activation and amitraz treatment.

claim: Pharmacological activation of Octβ2R by amitraz in vivo leads to toxicity and death.
source: which demonstrates that pharmacological activation of Octβ2R by amitraz in vivo leads to toxicity and finally to death.
evidence: This is inferred from the thermogenetic activation experiments that mimic amitraz effects.

claim: There were no differences in the OA EC50s among AmOctβ2R, VdOctβ2R, and DmOctβ2R.
source: We found that there were no differences in the AmOctβ2R, VdOctβ2R, and DmOctβ2R OA EC50s (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AmOctβ2R was 16-fold less sensitive to amitraz (EC50 = 1.2 µM) compared to VdOctβ2R.
source: Notably, compared to VdOctβ2R, we found that AmOctβ2R was 16-fold less sensitive to amitraz (EC50 = 1.2 µM) and 6-fold less sensitive to DPMF (EC50 = 43.4 nM; Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: AmOctβ2R was 6-fold less sensitive to DPMF (EC50 = 43.4 nM) compared to VdOctβ2R.
source: Notably, compared to VdOctβ2R, we found that AmOctβ2R was 16-fold less sensitive to amitraz (EC50 = 1.2 µM) and 6-fold less sensitive to DPMF (EC50 = 43.4 nM; Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: DmOctβ2R was threefold less sensitive to amitraz (EC50 = 242.1 nM) than VdOctβ2R.
source: In the case of DmOctβ2R, it was threefold less sensitive to amitraz (EC50 = 242.1 nM), but fivefold more sensitive to DPMF (EC50 = 1.4 nM) than VdOctβ2R (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: DmOctβ2R was fivefold more sensitive to DPMF (EC50 = 1.4 nM) than VdOctβ2R.
source: In the case of DmOctβ2R, it was threefold less sensitive to amitraz (EC50 = 242.1 nM), but fivefold more sensitive to DPMF (EC50 = 1.4 nM) than VdOctβ2R (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Metabolic detoxication may contribute to amitraz tolerance in flies.
source: suggesting that metabolic detoxication may contribute to amitraz tolerance in flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity to amitraz versus DPMF in DmOctβ2R.

claim: Both piperonyl butoxide (PBO) and S,S,S-tributylphosphorotrithioate (DEF) increased the toxicity of amitraz in survival assays.
source: Actually, we found that both piperonyl butoxide (PBO, a cytochrome P450s inhibitor) and S,S,S-tributylphosphorotrithioate (DEF, a model carboxylesterase inhibitor) increased the toxicity of amitraz in survival assays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Diethyl maleate (DEM) did not significantly change the toxicity of amitraz.
source: Diethyl maleate (DEM, a model glutathione-S-transferase inhibitor) did not significantly change the toxicity of amitraz (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fruit fly and honeybee employ different mechanisms to resist amitraz.
source: Thus, we suggest that the fruit fly and honeybee employ different mechanisms to resist amitraz.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of enzyme inhibitors and receptor sensitivity differences.

claim: All Drosophila and honeybee OA receptors except DmOAMB showed responses to amitraz and DPMF in nanomolar concentrations.
source: Notably, all but DmOAMB showed responses to amitraz and DPMF in nanomolar concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Amitraz and DPMF can bind all four OA receptors in fruit flies and honeybees.
source: These results indicate that amitraz and DPMF can bind all four OA receptors in fruit flies and honeybees
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological data showing nanomolar responses across receptors.

claim: The relative insensitivity of AmOctβ2R to amitraz is critical for selective toxicity.
source: further emphasizing that the relative insensitivity of AmOctβ2R to amitraz is critical for selective toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of receptor sensitivities and the fact that multiple receptors can bind amitraz.

claim: Amitraz is effective against mites and ticks, but safer for honeybees and bumblebees.
source: Amitraz is effective against mites and ticks, but safer for honeybees and for the bumblebee, Bombus terrestris (Marletto et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Three amino acids (E208, I335, I350) within the potential ligand-binding domain were unique to bees.
source: However, we found that three amino acids (E208, I335, I350) within the potential ligand-binding domain were unique to bees (Figure 5F; highlighted in green).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The engineered receptor AmOctβ2RE208V, I335T, I350V was more sensitive (EC50 = 440.0 nM) to amitraz than the wild-type AmOctβ2R (EC50 = 1.2 µM).
source: Interestingly, the engineered receptor (AmOctβ2RE208V, I335T, I350V, abbreviated to AmOctβ2RV3X) was more sensitive (EC50 = 440.0 nM) to amitraz than the wide-type AmOctβ2R (EC50 = 1.2 µM) (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The OA responses of AmOctβ2RV3X were not affected compared to wild-type AmOctβ2R.
source: while the OA responses were not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AmOctβ2RV3X showed no significant change in DPMF sensitivity compared to wild-type AmOctβ2R.
source: In contrast, AmOctβ2RV3X showed no significant change in DPMF sensitivity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The three residues E208, I335, and I350 are responsible for the resistance of honeybees to amitraz.
source: These results indicate that the three residues are responsible for the resistance of honeybees to amitraz.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased amitraz sensitivity of the mutant receptor with these residues replaced.

claim: Expression of AmOctβ2R or VdOctβ2R rescued the aggressive and locomotor behaviors induced by amitraz in octβ2R null mutant flies.
source: As expected, expression of AmOctβ2R or VdOctβ2R rescued the aggressive and locomotor behaviors induced by amitraz (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 'Varroa flies' (expressing VdOctβ2R) showed more aggression and hyperactivity than 'honeybee flies' (expressing AmOctβ2R).
source: Importantly, 'Varroa flies' showed more aggression and hyperactivity (Figure 6A and C–F)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 6A and 6C-F.

claim: There was no significant effect on the fighting latency between 'Varroa flies' and 'honeybee flies'.
source: while there was no significant effect on the fighting latency (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Flies expressing AmOctβ2RV3X displayed a robust increase in the lunging frequency and locomotion compared to flies expressing AmOctβ2R.
source: In addition, flies expressing AmOctβ2RV3X displayed a robust increase in the lunging frequency and locomotion than the 'honeybee flies' (Figure 6A and C–F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 6A and 6C-F.

claim: Three amino acid changes in honeybee Octβ2R partially phenocopy the amitraz-sensitive properties of the Varroa mites.
source: Therefore, these three amino acid changes in honeybee Octβ2R partially phenocopy the amitraz-sensitive properties of the Varroa mites.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data showing increased amitraz sensitivity in flies expressing the mutant receptor.

claim: A single mutation (I61F) in the cattle tick Octβ2R is associated with amitraz resistance.
source: A previous study found that a single mutation (I61F) in the cattle tick Octβ2R is associated with amitraz resistance (Corley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Mutation in the equivalent site (I40F) in Varroa Octβ2R did not reduce the potency of amitraz and DPMF.
source: However, we found that mutation in the equivalent site in Varroa Octβ2R did not reduce the potency of amitraz and DPMF.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The isoleucine residue in TM1 is unlikely to be involved in agonist binding since the traditional orthosteric site of class A GPCRs is close to a region that includes TM3, TM5, TM6, and TM7.
source: In addition, this isoleucine residue is in TM1 and is unlikely to be involved in agonist binding since the traditional orthosteric site of class A GPCRs is close to a region that includes TM3, TM5, TM6, and TM7 (Chan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature on GPCR structure.

claim: Reverse genetics using D. melanogaster has been a powerful approach to identify protein targets for insecticides.
source: Reverse genetics using D. melanogaster has been a powerful approach to identify protein targets for insecticides (Douris et al., 2016; Ffrench-Constant et al., 1993; Scott and Buchon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A Drosophila TRPV channel was identified as the target for pymetrozine and pyrifluquinazon using climbing assays.
source: For example, a recent study used climbing assays to identify a Drosophila TRPV channel as the target for two insecticides, pymetrozine and pyrifluquinazon (Nesterov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Octβ2R is conserved in invertebrates but absent in vertebrates.
source: Since Octβ2R is conserved in invertebrates but absent in vertebrates, it could be an ideal target for pest control.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the phylogenetic distribution of Octβ2R.

claim: The CYP9Q family can metabolize the flavonoid quercetin and detoxify the insecticides coumaphos and tau-fluvalinate.
source: For instance, the CYP9Q family can not only metabolize the flavonoid, quercetin, but can also detoxify the insecticides coumaphos and tau-fluvalinate (Mao et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The CYP9Q family can detoxify N-cyanoamidine neonicotinoids.
source: as well as N-cyanoamidine neonicotinoids (Manjon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: A voltage-gated sodium channel in bumblebees is resistant to tau-fluvalinate.
source: Interestingly, bumblebees may employ a different mechanism since a voltage-gated sodium channel, which is the molecular target of pyrethroids, is resistant to tau-fluvalinate (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Target-site insensitivity is the major mechanism for bees to resist amitraz.
source: Here we found that target-site insensitivity is the major mechanism for bees to resist amitraz.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological and genetic studies showing differential receptor sensitivity.

claim: Three amino acid replacements increased amitraz sensitivity without a cost to OA sensitivity.
source: Pharmacological and genetic studies revealed that three amino acids replacements increased amitraz sensitivity without a cost to OA sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Amitraz has been considered to be a pro-acaricide/insecticide for many years since it can be quickly metabolized to DPMF, DMF, DMA, and others.
source: Amitraz has been considered to be a pro-acaricide/insecticide for many years since it can be quickly metabolized to DPMF, 2,4-dimethylformanilide (DMF), 2,4-dimethylaniline (DMA), and others (Knowles and Hamed, 1989; Schuntner and Thompson, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both amitraz and DPMF are active in vivo.
source: Thus, it is thought that amitraz undergoes bioactivation in vivo to produce the active metabolite DPMF, although both drugs are active in vivo (Davenport et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Both amitraz and DPMF are potent Octβ2R agonists while DMF and DMA are not.
source: In this study, we found that both amitraz and DPMF are potent Octβ2R agonists while DMF and DMA are not (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: DPMF is 11 times more potent than amitraz on VdOctβ2R from Varroa mites.
source: DPMF is 11 times more potent than amitraz on VdOctβ2R from Varroa mites, which is consistent with a previous report using the silkworm orthologue (Kita et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data and citation to published research.

claim: DPMF is 28 times more potent than amitraz on AmOctβ2R from honeybees.
source: On the other hand, DPMF is 28 times more potent than amitraz on AmOctβ2R from honeybees.
evidence: This is inferred from the EC50 values reported for AmOctβ2R with amitraz (1.2 µM) and DPMF (43.4 nM).

claim: Amitraz content decreases rapidly to about 1/5 the level of DPMF in ticks and caterpillars.
source: Amitraz content decreases rapidly to about 1/5 the level of DPMF in ticks and caterpillars (Knowles and Hamed, 1989; Schuntner and Thompson, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Amitraz remains at a high level in honeybees even after 24 hr.
source: However, it remains at a high level in honeybees even after 24 hr (Hillier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Metabolic differences between mites and bees may further amplify the differential pharmacological effects and contribute to the bee's tolerance to amitraz.
source: Therefore, metabolic differences between mites and bees may further amplify the differential pharmacological effects and contribute to the bee's tolerance to amitraz.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in amitraz metabolism between species.

claim: Sublethal doses of insecticides may affect the physiology, cognitive function, and behavior of bees.
source: Growing evidence indicates that sublethal doses of insecticides may affect the physiology, cognitive function, and behavior of bees (Johnson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Octβ2R is involved in behaviors ranging from learning and memory to ovulation, foraging, and sleep in Drosophila.
source: Genetic studies on Drosophila have revealed that Octβ2R is involved in behaviors ranging from learning and memory (Burke et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2013) to ovulation (Lim et al., 2014), foraging (Koon et al., 2011), and sleep (Deng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Amitraz significantly synergizes the toxic effects of tau-fluvalinate and coumaphos on honeybees.
source: Amitraz significantly synergizes the toxic effects of tau-fluvalinate and coumaphos on honeybees (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Amitraz shows selective synergistic effects for neonicotinoids and pyrethroids against mosquito larvae.
source: Amitraz also shows selective synergistic effects for neonicotinoids and pyrethroids against mosquito larvae (Ahmed and Matsumura, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Some plant-derived essential oils are insecticidal and act on OA receptors.
source: Some plant-derived essential oils are insecticidal and act on OA receptors (Jankowska et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.
